subject: technology
unit_title: Applied Cybersecurity, Privacy Engineering, and Risk
essential_question: How do we design for privacy and security before there is anything to attack?
standards: Michigan Computer Science: Networks and the Internet — Cybersecurity
project_brief: Produce a security and privacy engineering review for a fictional system with a risk register and an incident-response plan; all work stays in a sandbox and no live system is tested. This is the grade 12 culminating project for "Applied Cybersecurity, Privacy Engineering, and Risk" (ma-g12-technology-u03, unit 3), built around risk assessment and threat modeling at scale, secure architecture and defense in depth, privacy by design and data minimization, incident response and disclosure ethics, and authorization scope and legal boundaries. Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to risk assessment and threat modeling at scale, secure architecture and defense in depth, privacy by design and data minimization, and incident response and disclosure ethics, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
requirements: Address every topic listed for this unit: risk assessment and threat modeling at scale, secure architecture and defense in depth, privacy by design and data minimization, incident response and disclosure ethics, authorization scope and legal boundaries, and sandboxed defensive exercises.

Meet the performance task as written: Produce a security and privacy engineering review for a fictional system with a risk register and an incident-response plan; all work stays in a sandbox and no live system is tested.
Show your work or process, not just a final result — a process note, sketch log, commit history, or draft trail.
Complete the checklist in this package before submitting.
primary_task: Collect or use a small, fictional or already-approved data set related to risk assessment and threat modeling at scale, secure architecture and defense in depth, privacy by design and data minimization, and incident response and disclosure ethics, and turn it into a labeled visual with a one-paragraph, evidence-based conclusion.
test_or_check_criteria: Every claim or design choice in the submission can be traced to risk assessment and threat modeling at scale or another named topic from this unit — nothing is left unexplained.
The submission runs, displays, or demonstrates correctly on at least two different sample inputs or scenarios the student chooses.
No real password, API key, account credential, precise location, or other real personal/system data appears anywhere in the submission — fictional or sandbox examples only.
The student can explain, in their own words, why each step or decision was made, not just that it works.

presentation_and_privacy.sandbox_and_credentials_note: This project never touches a real account, a real password or API key, a live production system, or another person's real data. Use fictional names, sandbox environments, local files, or already-approved sample data throughout. Submit code, screenshots of your own sandbox, diagrams, or a written walkthrough — a live public deployment is never required.

copyright_and_authorship: The final submitted work must remain your own authorship. A parent, tutor, or AI assistant may help you plan, explain a concept, demonstrate a technique, or give feedback on a draft, but may not produce the graded work itself. Never request, store, or submit a real password, API key, access token, or other real credential; use only fictional accounts and sandboxed or offline systems.
remediation: If the project stalls, step back to the smallest version of the task: rebuild just the part covering risk assessment and threat modeling at scale in isolation, using a worked example from this unit as a model, then re-attach it to the full project once that smaller piece works and you can explain why.
extension: Once the core project is working, extend it to handle a new constraint or edge case related to secure architecture and defense in depth, or compare two different approaches to the same problem and explain the real tradeoff between them in your own words.
